charts.title: Gross Profit, Operating Income & Net Income
Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC): equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC): the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

efficiencyPrePcl.title: Pre-PCL profit and efficiency ratio
efficiencyPrePcl.content:
Pre-provision, pre-credit-loss (PrePCL) profit is revenue less non-interest expense, before any provision for credit losses -- the bank's earnings power before the credit cycle shows up. The efficiency ratio is non-interest expense divided by revenue: the lower the better, since it is the share of every revenue dollar spent running the bank.

For Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC): PrePCL profit has grown every year since FY2023 (from roughly C$9.0bn to C$13.3bn in FY2025) while the efficiency ratio improved from 61.5% to 54.4% over the same period -- cost discipline alongside growth, not growth funded by rising costs.

What to watch:

  • Efficiency ratio drifting above the mid-50s%, which would signal costs outrunning revenue
  • PrePCL profit growth that is really just revenue growth, with the efficiency ratio flat or worsening
  • The gap between PrePCL profit and reported net income is the credit-loss provision -- widening in a downturn even if PrePCL itself holds up

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC): the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC): the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC): the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC): CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC): the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC): the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC): the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

dcf.base_sublabel: Owner FCF — after SBC, interest income & leases
dcf.model_approach_note: No driver changed. Root-caused the trip to a currency-direction defect in scripts/sanity_check.py historical_table() for this ticker: inputs.fx_rate (0.7019, CAD->USD) follows dcf_engine.py's documented convention (currency->quote_currency, used to produce the USD headline IV from the CAD-denominated model -- confirmed against tests/test_dcf_engine.py::TestCurrency and the WISE.L/APA fixtures). sanity_check.py::historical_table applies the SAME stored fx_rate in the OPPOSITE direction (quote_currency->currency, per its own docstring and tests/test_sanity_check.py::test_the_fx_rate_is_quote_to_reporting), to convert the fetched USD NYSE price series into CAD before dividing by CAD book value/EPS. Multiplying a USD price by the CAD->USD rate instead of dividing by it produced FY-end anchor prices roughly half the real NYSE close (e.g. FY2025 58.17 vs an actual ~82-86 close), understating the entire historical P/B and P/E band. This is a latent defect affecting any ticker with currency != quote_currency, not specific to CM -- left unfixed here because it is shared, test-pinned infrastructure (both conventions are asserted by passing tests) that needs a maintainer decision, not a one-ticker patch. Recomputed the comparison by hand on a consistent CAD basis (TSX close / CAD book&EPS) instead: see valuation_philosophy.sanity_check_response for the full walkthrough.
